global.headline: IRAN REJECTS IRAQI-BROKERED CEASEFIRE AS TRUMP WEIGHS "MASSIVE" NEW ATTACK; MOVES TO PAY SHIPPING DAMAGES FROM IRAN'S OWN FROZEN FUNDS
summary: Iran rejected a US ceasefire proposal hand-carried to Tehran by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who met President Masoud Pezeshkian, chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and FM Abbas Araghchi during his first official visit to Iran. Iranian officials told the New York Times they were not interested in a "temporary deal" that left control of the Strait of Hormuz unresolved. CENTCOM completed a 13th consecutive night of strikes (concluded 9pm ET Thursday, roughly two hours fifteen minutes) on Iranian command centres, drone-storage facilities, communications networks, coastal surveillance and maritime capabilities; Iranian provincial authorities in Khuzestan reported 4 killed and 5 wounded near Ahvaz. Trump told Israel's Channel 12 he is considering a "massive attack" larger than the operation that opened this phase of the war, though he stressed no final order has been given.

Trump separately said on Truth Social that "from now on and until further notice," any damage to ships or cargo from Iranian attacks in the Gulf will be compensated using Iranian funds frozen and held under US control — assets independently estimated at $100–120 billion globally, of which the US itself holds a relatively small share (roughly $2 billion), with the balance frozen in third countries including Iraq, Qatar, Japan and China. Iran's FM Araghchi called it an "incendiary precedent," warning that "seizing another nation's assets to pay for unrelated future claims" sets a dangerous template. Brent crude briefly topped $100/barrel on the rejected-ceasefire news and continuing Houthi attacks on Saudi-bound shipping, then fell roughly 4% to settle near $97 — its steepest one-day drop since late June — as traders weighed the diplomatic rebuff against no fresh single flashpoint.

Separately, the New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported this week that Trump switched from the new Qatari-donated Boeing 747-8 to the older, better-defended Air Force One when leaving Turkey earlier this month, after Israeli intelligence flagged a "specific" Iranian-proxy plot timed to his NATO-summit visit to Ankara; the US Secret Service requested the switch as a precaution, and some officials cautioned the threat's operational credibility was unconfirmed.
global.geopolitical: A rejected ceasefire, a fresh threat to seize Iran's own frozen assets, and Trump openly weighing an attack "bigger than" the operation that started this round together mark the sharpest one-day hardening of the US position since the truce collapsed in early July, with Iraq's mediation now the second regional channel (after Qatar/Egypt/Pakistan's 21 July proposal) to fail.
global.socioeconomic: Oil's round trip — briefly above $100 then a 4% same-day retreat — underscores how unstable energy pricing has become for import-dependent Singapore just as households absorb a record Q3 electricity tariff; the frozen-assets threat also raises the stakes for any state or shipper with exposure to Iranian assets held in third countries, a new and untested category of war-related financial risk.

global.headline: TRUMP THREATENS EU WITH FRESH TARIFFS AND A SECTION 301 PROBE OVER $1B GOOGLE FINE
summary: The European Commission fined Google €890 million (about US$1 billion) for breaching the Digital Markets Act, finding the company steered Google Play and Search users toward its own services over rivals' — the EU's latest in a decade-long string of penalties against the company, including a 2025 €2.9 billion adtech fine currently under appeal. Trump responded on Truth Social that the EU "will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct," announcing he would "immediately initiate a 301 Investigation" into what he called the bloc "ROBBING" American tech firms, and said he expects a "substantial tariff" on the EU "at the earliest possible moment."

A Section 301 probe under the 1974 Trade Act would let Washington investigate the EU's antitrust enforcement as an unfair trade practice and retaliate with new duties — a distinct, EU-specific escalation layered on top of the 10–12.5% global tariff reset that took effect across 80+ countries on 24 July.
global.geopolitical: Treating a domestic EU antitrust ruling against a US company as grounds for a trade investigation blurs competition policy and trade policy in a way Brussels has resisted for years, and tests whether the EU holds its regulatory line under renewed tariff threat so soon after absorbing the broader global tariff reset.
global.socioeconomic: A US-EU trade fight compounds an already volatile tariff and oil-price backdrop for trade-dependent economies like Singapore, adding another source of uncertainty to global supply chains and investment flows even though Singapore itself is not a direct party to this specific dispute.

global.headline: SPAIN DECLARES FIRST-EVER WILDFIRE NATIONAL EMERGENCY; 200,000+ FLEE FIRES SWEEPING FRANCE AND SPAIN
summary: Spain's Interior Ministry declared a National Emergency — the country's first ever linked to a wildfire — covering parts of Madrid region and Ávila province late Thursday, handing operational command to the elite Military Emergency Unit (UME) as multiple blazes erupted simultaneously; two fires west of Madrid merged into a single blaze that has charred roughly 30 sq km and is, per officials, "beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain." More than 1,000 soldiers, 270+ emergency personnel and 40 ground units have been deployed; at least 18,000 people were evacuated from the merged Madrid-area fire alone, with a further 1,500 evacuated in Ávila. A man in Tres Cantos, a Madrid suburb, died of burns covering 98% of his body trying to save horses at an equestrian centre; separately, three firefighters have died battling wildfires across Spain this year, and more than 100,000 hectares have burned nationwide.

In France, a wildfire reached the outskirts of Bordeaux, prompting President Macron to order a military mobilisation and the evacuation of the Cap Ferret peninsula; combined evacuations across France and Spain now exceed 200,000 people, with heatwave conditions across southern Europe driving simultaneous fires in Italy as well.
global.geopolitical: A first-of-its-kind national wildfire emergency in Spain, alongside a French military mobilisation to defend a major city, marks an escalation in how far European governments are now willing to go operationally in response to climate-driven disasters, and adds pressure for EU-level firefighting and heat-adaptation coordination.
global.socioeconomic: Beyond the immediate human toll, mass evacuations and infrastructure strain in two major European economies during peak summer tourism season carry direct costs for regional GDP and insurance markets — a preview of the kind of climate-driven disruption cost-of-living and insurance-pricing debates increasingly reference globally, Singapore included.

global.headline: RUSSIAN MISSILES KILL 10 AT UKRAINIAN DEFENCE-INDUSTRY EXHIBITION NEAR KYIV
summary: Russia fired three ballistic missiles at a drone-technology exhibition at a training ground on the Zhytomyr highway near Kyiv on Friday, with only one intercepted; the daytime strike killed 10 people and injured around 100, President Zelensky said, at an event attended by leading figures from Ukraine's defence industry. Russia's Defence Ministry said it deliberately targeted the exhibition, claiming it displayed drones intended for strikes on Russian civilian targets. Separately, Russian glide-bomb strikes killed 5 people in the eastern city of Sloviansk the same day, bringing Friday's nationwide death toll to at least 15.
global.geopolitical: Deliberately targeting a defence-industry exhibition — rather than a production site or military base — signals Russia is now willing to strike gatherings of Ukraine's arms-sector personnel directly, a new category of target that widens the war's reach into Ukraine's defence-industrial base beyond factories and depots.
global.socioeconomic: An attack aimed squarely at the people building and selling Ukraine's drone capability threatens to disrupt the domestic defence-industrial expansion Kyiv has relied on as Western arms pledges face their own funding and delivery pressures.

global.headline: ICC MEMBER STATES REMOVE CHIEF PROSECUTOR KARIM KHAN OVER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT — A FIRST IN THE COURT'S HISTORY
summary: Member states of the International Criminal Court voted 82 of 125 to formally dismiss Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan on Friday over findings of sexual misconduct involving a female aide — the first time the ICC has ever removed a sitting chief prosecutor. Khan, 56, has consistently denied the allegations, and his lawyers called the removal process "illegal, procedurally unfair, and not supported by evidence." His dismissal triggers the process of electing a successor, a vote not expected until next year; Mame Mandiaye Niang takes over in the interim. All existing ICC arrest warrants — including those issued under Khan's tenure — remain in force, since only ICC judges, not the prosecutor's office, have authority to lift them.
global.geopolitical: An unprecedented removal of the court's top prosecutor, mid-tenure and amid several of the ICC's highest-profile and most politically contested cases, raises fresh questions about the court's institutional stability and independence at a moment several major powers are already contesting its jurisdiction and authority.
global.socioeconomic: Limited direct economic bearing, though prolonged uncertainty at the top of the world's principal international-crimes tribunal complicates the legal backdrop for states and companies navigating sanctions, war-crimes exposure and cross-border accountability questions tied to the conflicts this pipeline already tracks.

singapore.headline: TRUMP HITS SINGAPORE WITH 12.5% TARIFF OVER FORCED-LABOUR ALLEGATIONS; MTI REJECTS THE CLAIM
summary: Singapore is among 54 economies named in the US Trade Representative's Section 301 forced-labour determination, published 23 July after a probe launched in March covering 60 economies; it faces a new 12.5% tariff — among the highest in the reset — that took effect 24 July 2026 at 12:01am US Eastern time, on top of the broader 10-12.5% global tariff reset covering roughly 99.4% of US imports. USTR found Singapore had allegedly "failed to adopt and effectively enforce" a prohibition on trading in goods made with forced labour; about one-third of Singapore's domestic exports to the US are affected.

Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry firmly rejected the allegation, stating Singapore "has not adopted any acts, policies, and practices which are unreasonable or discriminatory, or which have burdened or restricted US commerce," and that there is no evidence linking Singapore to forced-labour supply chains for goods exported to the US. MTI said it will continue engaging USTR to explore options. Singapore was named in the same forced-labour probe alongside Malaysia and dozens of other economies in March; both governments have consistently rejected the underlying allegation.
singapore.geopolitical: Naming Singapore — a close US security and trade partner with no history of forced-labour findings against it in this probe's public record — under the same forced-labour rationale used against dozens of other economies suggests the justification is being applied close to uniformly across the board rather than targeted at specific evidence, straining the bilateral trade relationship regardless of the small number of contested product lines.
singapore.socioeconomic: A 12.5% tariff on roughly a third of Singapore's US-bound exports lands directly on an externally-oriented economy already absorbing record COE prices and a record Q3 electricity tariff, adding a fresh headwind for MTI's 2026 growth forecast and for MAS's policy calculus ahead of any further tightening review.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE POLICE AND FBI SIGN MOU TO JOINTLY TACKLE MONEY LAUNDERING, CYBERSCAMS AND FRAUD
summary: The Singapore Police Force and the US Federal Bureau of Investigation signed a memorandum of understanding at the US Embassy in Singapore on 24 July, formalising cooperation on online scams, cyber-enabled fraud and money laundering. SPF deputy commissioner of investigation and intelligence Zhang Weihan and FBI assistant director for the Criminal Division Heith R. Janke signed on behalf of their agencies.

SPF said the MOU "symbolises the SPF and the FBI's shared resolve and strengthening of our partnership to interdict and to disrupt criminal syndicates targeting citizens"; Zhang added that "these crimes are inherently borderless, and it is only through close collaboration with trusted international partners like the FBI that we can effectively disrupt and dismantle the criminal networks behind them."
singapore.geopolitical: Deepens US-Singapore law-enforcement cooperation on transnational financial crime at a time Singapore has faced sustained scrutiny over its role as a regional money-laundering and scam-syndicate hub, following the S$3b money-laundering case and repeated cross-border scam operations tracked through this pipeline.
singapore.socioeconomic: Closer FBI ties give Singapore's police additional reach into US-based scam infrastructure and mule networks, potentially improving recovery rates for local victims of cyber-enabled fraud, a persistent and costly problem for households here.

singapore.headline: GIC'S THREE ANTHROPIC BETS IN A YEAR LAND IT A STAKE IN A ~S$1.2 TRILLION AI COMPANY
summary: GIC has invested in AI company Anthropic three times over roughly a year: an initial, undisclosed investment around September 2025; leading a US$30b (S$38.7b) Series G round in February 2026 that valued Anthropic at US$380b; and co-leading a US$65b (S$83.9b) Series H round in May 2026 that valued the company at US$965b (roughly S$1.2 trillion). Anthropic's run-rate revenue rose from about US$9b at end-2025 to roughly US$47b (S$60.7b) by May 2026 — more than fivefold in under a year. GIC has not disclosed the size of its resulting stake.
singapore.geopolitical: Repeated, escalating commitments to a single US AI lab underline how central American frontier-AI companies have become to sovereign-wealth AI strategy globally, reinforcing Singapore's stated ambition (per Temasek's own AI-allocation ramp, tracked separately) to build meaningful exposure to the sector rather than simply diversify around it.
singapore.socioeconomic: A stake in a company now valued near S$1.2 trillion materially raises the concentration and volatility of GIC's AI-sector exposure ahead of any correction in AI valuations, a risk GIC's own public commentary on portfolio resilience has flagged in general terms without singling out any one holding.

singapore.headline: PRIVATE HOME RENTS UP 0.7%, PRICES UP 0.5% IN Q2 AS VACANCY RATE CLIMBS: URA
summary: URA's Q2 2026 data show private residential rents rose 0.7% quarter-on-quarter, faster than Q1's 0.3% gain, led by landed properties (+2.7% vs +0.1% in Q1) while non-landed rents were flat at +0.4%. The overall private home price index rose 0.5% QoQ, easing from Q1's 0.9% gain, with landed and Core Central Region non-landed properties driving the gains, partly offset by declines in the Rest of Central Region and Outside Central Region non-landed segments. The vacancy rate climbed to 6.4% as at end-Q2, up from 6.2% in Q1, even as both rents and prices rose.
singapore.socioeconomic: Rents and prices rising together with vacancy — an unusual combination — suggests landlords are holding firm on asking rents despite more unsold/unoccupied stock, adding a further cost-of-living data point for MAS to weigh alongside record COE prices and the record Q3 electricity tariff ahead of any further policy tightening.

word.definition: The restoration of something lost or stolen to its rightful owner, or compensation for injury or loss.
word.etymology: From Latin restitutio ("a restoring, replacing"), from restituere, "to set up again, restore," from re- ("again") + statuere ("to set up, establish").
word.example: Trump declared that Iran's own frozen assets — not US funds — would furnish restitution for any ships or cargo damaged by future attacks in the Gulf, a formula Tehran's foreign minister branded an "incendiary precedent" rather than justice.
